priorVersion.title: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021)
priorVersion.summary: Only the class members with the relevant concrete injury could recover damages in federal court; the Court distinguished inaccurate files from disseminated reports.
priorVersion.notes: The assigned note expressly states that the Court did not decide whether every class member must establish standing before certification. Preserve that reservation. This account is limited to the casebook’s short treatment, not the full opinion.

sections.Parties: A class of consumers sued TransUnion under the Fair Credit Reporting Act over misleading information in their credit files.
sections.Material Facts: TransUnion had associated the consumers with a government list of specially designated nationals, which included terrorists and other persons presenting national-security concerns. The class contained 8,185 consumers, but the parties stipulated that reports concerning only 1,853 had been disseminated to potential creditors during the relevant period. The remaining 6,332 files had not been provided to third parties in that period. The class alleged failures of reasonable accuracy procedures and required disclosures.
sections.Procedural History: The district court certified the class, and the jury awarded statutory and punitive damages. The Ninth Circuit reduced the punitive award but found standing for the class. The Supreme Court reversed the standing determination in part and remanded for reconsideration of certification.
sections.Issue: Did all class members have Article III standing to recover individual damages because their statutory rights were violated?
sections.Holding: No. The majority found concrete reputational harm for the disseminated reports and insufficient concrete harm for the undisseminated files on the theory before it.
sections.Reasoning: The majority required the parties invoking federal jurisdiction to show the injury that Article III demands. A class-action device cannot confer a damages remedy on a person who lacks that jurisdictional injury. Dissemination supplied the concrete reputational harm relevant here; the inaccurate internal files did not establish the same harm merely by existing. The Court distinguished Congress’s creation of a statutory cause of action from the constitutional conditions of federal adjudication.

learning.why: Only the class members with the relevant concrete injury could recover damages in federal court; the Court distinguished inaccurate files from disseminated reports.

topics.cp-standing: Every class member recovering individual damages needed a concrete injury satisfying Article III.
topics.cp-class-jurisdiction: Class certification did not automatically supply standing for uninjured members.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: A statutory violation and an Article III injury were distinct questions in the majority’s analysis.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Thomas, joined by three Justices, dissented. He would have treated violation of the individualized private rights created by Congress as sufficient injury for these consumers.
